findings.where: Screen 10 answer buttons, the b² − 4ac readout on every screen (COUNT map), FINISH and the practice list
findings.what: The nature of the roots is said as "two roots" and "one repeated root", not SQA's "two real and distinct roots" and "one repeated real root" that the brief chose, so the lesson teaches the "incomplete description of the nature of the roots" that SQA 2023 marks down (brief section 4), and "two roots" also sits oddly beside the closing point that a negative discriminant still has two complex roots; when the words are lengthened, give the readout's word its own line, because "two real and distinct roots" right-aligned at x = 328 would run into "b² − 4ac = 36 − 8 = 28" at 360 px.

findings.where: Explain, paragraph 2 ("A number squared makes this when it is the square root either way")
findings.what: This sentence is where the ± comes from, which the brief names as the most common error, yet it is hard to parse; say "a square equals this number only when what is squared is its positive or its negative square root, so x + b ÷ 2a = ±√(b² − 4ac) ÷ 2a", and say √(4a²) is "2a or −2a, whichever is positive" rather than "2a or −2a".

The text says each line follows from the one above, but line 1 to line 2 (take a out, halve b ÷ a, add and remove the corner a times) and line 2 to line 3 (move the plain part across, write c as 4ac ÷ 4a, divide by a) are several moves each; only the reading text shows them, so add a short note line or a sentence pointing to it.

findings.where: Whole lesson against the brief's lesson 5 row
findings.what: The fireworks equation 4.90t² − 14.3t − 20.0 = 0 (OpenStax, with the lesson's own 3.95 s and why OpenStax prints 3.96 s) and the screen that checks a root with the calculator's equation solver were both promised and are missing, so lesson 7, whose brief row refers back to "the fireworks' negative time", must now introduce the fireworks itself, or a screen should be added here.

The brief's most-cited slip, dropping the ± (Edexcel 2021), never appears as a wrong option in a puzzle (the options are sign flips, measuring from 0 and putting only the root over 2a); offering "Just −1" on screen 2 or "Just 5" on screen 11 would let him meet it as well as read about it in the common mistakes.

"−4ac turns positive when just one of a and c is negative (with a = −1 and c = −2 it is −8)" gives the both-negative counter-case as if it were an example of the rule; write "(with both negative, a = −1 and c = −2, it is −8)".

findings.where: Screen 9 (Set a, b and c), text
findings.what: The demonstration sinks the upside-down U to c = −6 and its roots vanish, the opposite of screen 7's "lift the curve", but the words do not say so; one clause ("for an upside-down U it is lowering it that loses the roots") stops him generalising "lift = fewer roots" to every quadratic.

findings.where: Screen 12 (two decimal places), working after a right answer
findings.what: Unlike screens 2, 4 and 11, the solved working stops at "x is about 0.18 or −1.85" without putting a root back (3 × 0.18² + 5 × 0.18 − 1 is about 0, give or take the rounding), although the brief says every solve ends by trying the root in the rule.

findings.where: Screen 2 before Check (360 light and dark moved pictures)
findings.what: The arrowheads stop 6 units short of their ends, so with no root dots drawn the arrows seem to end at about −4.8 and −1.2 rather than −5 and −1; the "2" labels carry the meaning, but on a screen with no dots the tips could reach the root exactly.

findings.where: Screens 2 and 13 at 360 px, between the key and the answer buttons
findings.what: About 150 px of blank space is reserved for working that only appears after Check, which pushes Check and Why? below the first phone screenful; a shorter reserve, or showing the working beneath the buttons, would keep the puzzle in one view.

The lesson writes −b ÷ 2a to mean −b ÷ (2a), and its spot-the-slip is itself about what the bottom applies to, so a single line saying to type the bottom in brackets on a calculator, ÷ (2 × 3), would stop the same slip happening on his calculator.
